StringWithMarkup.String: Peroxyacetyl nitrate exits in equilibrium with the radical intermediates from which it is formed, thereby existing as a sink or source depending on the concentration of the peroxyacetyl radical and NO2 in the atmosphere. This dissociation occurs with a lifetime of 30 minutes at 25 °C. At high NO2/NO ratios, peroxyacetyl nitrate is regenerated following each dissociation of peroxyacetyl nitrate molecule; however at NO2/NO = 3, a molecule is regenerated only one out of two dissociations; this is due to rapid reaction with NO which has a rate constant three times faster than the reaction with NO2. When peroxyacetyl nitrate does react with NO, it will generate radicals which initiate additional hydrocarbon consumption and NO oxidation.

PAN concentrations used in the 4 week study were 0, 0.9, 4.1, or 11.8 ppm; concentrations used in the 13 week study were 0, 0.2, 1.0 or 4.6 ppm. In the 4 week study, exposure to 11.8 ppm caused elevated mortality, hematocrit values, red blood cell counts and lung weight. In addition, exposure resulted in abnormal behavior, growth retardation, severe inflammation, epithelial metaplasia and hyperplasia in the respiratory tract. Minimal behavioral disturbance, transient growth retardation, slightly increased lung weights and slight histopathological changes in the respiratory tract were noted at 4.1 ppm. No treatment related effects were noted at 0.9 ppm. Exposure to 4.6 ppm in the 13 week study resulted in changes similar to those found at 11.8 ppm in the 4 week study, with the exception that elevated mortality was not observed. StringWithMarkup.String: Peroxyacetyl nitrate is formed as a result of atmospheric photochemical reactions of hydrocarbons (typically resulting from industrial and domestic activities) in the presence of NOx. It is one of the Greenhouse Gases. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 29.2 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates peroxyacetyl nitrate will exist solely as a vapor in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase peroxyacetyl nitrate will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 380 days. Peroxyacetyl nitrate is very stable at low temperatures but does decompose at higher temperatures to release NO2. Peroxyacetyl nitrate was photolyzed readily when irradiated with light at wavelengths <300 nm and therefore may be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, peroxyacetyl nitrate is expected to have very high mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 4. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon a Henry's Law constant of 2.78X10-4 atm-cu m/mole. Peroxyacetyl nitrate may volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its vapor pressure. However, mobility and volatilization may be attenuated by the polar nature of this compound. Biodegradation data were not available. If released into water, peroxyacetyl nitrate is not expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. Volatilization from water surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's Henry's Law constant. Estimated volatilization half-lives for a model river and model lake are 7 hours and 5 days. An estimated BCF of 3 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Hydrolysis may be an important environmental fate process since this compound contains functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions. The most likely pathway by which the general public is exposed to peroxyacetyl nitrate is by inhalation due to the formation of this substance as a result of industrial and domestic activities. (SRC)

StringWithMarkup.String: ATMOSPHERIC FATE: According to a model of gas/particle partitioning of semivolatile organic compounds in the atmosphere(1), peroxyacetyl nitrate, which has a vapor pressure of 29.2 mm Hg at 25 °C(2), is expected to exist solely as a vapor in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase peroxyacetyl nitrate is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals(SRC); the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 380 days(SRC), calculated from its rate constant of 1.0X10-13 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(3). Peroxyacetyl nitrate is very stable at low temperatures but does decompose at higher temperatures to release NO2; whether photolysis can compete with thermal decomposition is still of interest(4). Peroxyacetyl nitrate exits in equilibrium with the radical intermediates from which it is formed, thereby existing as a sink or source depending on the concentration of the peroxyacetyl radical and NO2 in the atmosphere(5). When peroxyacetyl nitrate does react with NO, it will generate radicals which initiate additional hydrocarbon consumption and NO oxidation(5). Therefore, peroxyacetyl nitrate plays an important role in atmospheric chemistry and has a large effect on ozone formation(5). Peroxyacetyl nitrate was photolyzed readily when irradiated with light at wavelengths <300 nm(2) and therefore may be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight(SRC). The compound has been identified as one of the main components of photochemical smog throughout the planet(2).

StringWithMarkup.String: Peroxyacetyl nitrate is very stable at low temperatures but does decompose at higher temperatures to release NO2; long lifetimes of the order of a year or more at low temperatures of approximately 215 K and very short lifetimes of <1 hour at higher temperatures around 298 K (25 °C)(1). Whether photolysis can compete with thermal decomposition is still of interest(1). Peroxyacetyl nitrate exits in equilibrium with the radical intermediates from which it is formed, thereby existing as a sink or source depending on the concentration of the peroxyacetyl radical and NO2 in the atmosphere(2). This dissociation occurs with a lifetime of 30 minutes at 25 °C(2). At high NO2/NO ratios, peroxyacetyl nitrate is regenerated following each dissociation of peroxyacetyl nitrate molecule; however at NO2/NO = 3, a molecule is regenerated only one out of two dissociations; this is due to rapid reaction with NO which has a rate constant three times faster than the reaction with NO2(2). When peroxyacetyl nitrate does react with NO, it will generate radicals which initiate additional hydrocarbon consumption and NO oxidation(2). Therefore, peroxyacetyl nitrate plays an important role in atmospheric chemistry and has a large effect on ozone formation(2). Peroxyacetyl nitrate was stable when irradiated with light at wavelengths >300 nm; below 300 nm, the compound was photolyzed readily as indicated by the identification of an acetylperoxy radical(3). The photolysis of organic nitrates through absorption of solar radiation in the near UV region appears to be an important atmospheric loss process(4). The photodissociation rate constant for peroxyacetyl nitrate is 0.061X10+6/sec to 0.21X10+6/sec(5).

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.

StringWithMarkup.String: Peroxyacetyl nitrate has been identified as one of the main components of photochemical smog throughout the planet(1,6). The reaction of acetaldehyde with the OH free radical in urban atmospheres leads directly to the formation of the peroxyacetyl radical which in turn reacts with NO2 to form peroxyacetyl nitrate(2). In a field study conducted to assess the atmospheric impacts of ethanol fuel use, peroxyacetyl nitrate was shown to increase following the use of 10% ethanol fuel over the 1994 and 1995 winters in Albuquerque, NM as compared to summer levels in 1993, before the use of ethanol fuels(2). Peroxyacetyl nitrate concentrations in irradiated wood smoke from North Carolina oak species were 52 ppb (Apr 18), 174 ppb (Mar 7), and 232 ppb (Mar 28); NOx was added to burn chambers to a concentration of approx 0.6 ppm(3). The average air emission of peroxyacetyl nitrate from stationary sources in The Netherlands is 283 tons/yr(4). In a study evaluating the photochemical air pollution potential of representative 1996 America automobiles, peroxyacetyl nitrate was produced upon irradiation of exhaust from Chevelles not equipped with clean-air devices(5).
